source_text: Afuit ergo ab his fingendi uoluntas et astutia, quoniam rudes fuerunt. aut quis possit indoctus apta inter se et cohaerentia fingere, cum philosophorum doctissimi, Plato et Aristoteles et Epicurus et Zenon, ipsi sibi repugnantia et contraria dixerint ? haec est enim mendaciorum natura, ut cohaerere non possint. illorum autem traditio quia uera est, quadrat undique ac sibi tota consentit et ideo persuadet, quia constanti ratione subfulta est. non igitur quaestus et commodi gratia religionem istam conmenti sunt, quippe qui et praeceptis et re ipsa eam uitam secuti sint, quae et uoluptatibus caret et omnia quae habentur in bonis spernit, et qui non tantum pro fide mortem subierint, sed etiam morituros esse se et scierint et praedixerint et postea uniuersos qui eorum disciplinam secuti essent acerba et nefanda passuros. ipsum autem Christum adfirmauit a Iudaeis fugatum collecta nongentorum hominum manu latrocinia fecisse. quis tantae auctoritati audeat repugnare? credamus hoc plane, nam fortasse illi hoc in somnis Apollo aliquis nuntiauit. tot semper latrones perierunt et cottidie pereunt, utique multos et ipse damnasti: quis eorum post crucem suam non dicam deus, sed homo appellatus est? uerum tu forsitan ex eo credidisti, quia uos homicidam . Martem consecrastis ut deum: quod tamen non fecissetis, si illum Ariopagitae in crucem sustulissent. idem cum facta eius mirabilia destrueret nec tamen negaret, uoluit ostendere Apollonium uel paria uel etiam maiora fecisse. mirum quod Apuleium praetermisit, cuius solent et multa et mira memorari. cur igitur, o delirum caput, nemo Apollonium pro deo colit? nisi forte tu solus, illo scilicet deo dignus, cum quo te in sempiternum uerus deus puniet. si magus Christus, quia mirabilia fecit, peritior utique Apollonius, qui ut describis cum Domitianus eum punire uellet, repente in iudicio non conparuit. quam ille qui et conprehensus est et cruci adfixus. at enim ex hoc ipso fortasse insolentiam Christi uoluit arguere, quod deum se constituerit, ut ille uerecundior fuisse uideatur, qui cum maiora faceret, ut hic putat, tamen id sibi non adrogauerit. omitto nunc ipsa opera conparare, quia in secundo et in superiore libro de fraude ac praestigiis artis magicae dixi. nego esse quemquam qui non optet in primis id sibi post mortem contingere quod etiam reges maximi concupiscunt. cur enim sibi homines sepulchra magnifica, cur statuas, cur imagines conparant? cur aliquibus claris factis aut etiam pro ciuibus morte suscepta student opiniones hominum promereri? cur denique ipse ingenii tui monumentum hoc detestabile stultitia tamquam caeno aedificatum constituere uoluisti, nisi quod inmortalitatem de memoria nominis speras? stultum igitur est id putare Apollonium noluisse quod optaret utique, si posset, quia nemo est qui inmortalitatem recuset, maxime cum eum dicas et adoratum esse a quibusdam sicut deum et simulacrum eius sub Herculis Alexicaci nomine constitutum ab Ephesiis etiam nunc honorari. non potuit ergo post mortem deus credi, quia et hominem et magum fuisse constabat, et ideo alieni nominis titulo adfectauit diuinitatem, quia suo nec poterat nec audebat. noster uero et potuit deus credi, quia magus non fuit, et creditus est, quia uere fuit. non in quit hoc dico, idcirco Apollonium non haberi deum, quia noluerit, sed ut appareat nos sapientiores esse, qui mirabilibus factis non statim fidem diuinitatis adiunximus, quam uos, qui ob exigua portenta deum credidistis. non est mirum si tu, qui a dei sapientia longe remotus es, nihil prorsus intellegis eorum quae legisti, cum Iudaei, qui a principio prophetas lectitauerant quibusque sacramentum dei fuerat adsignatum, tamen quid legerent ignorauerint. disce igitur, si quid tibi cordis est, non idcirco a nobis deum creditum, quia mirabilia fecit, sed quia uidimus in eo facta esse omnia quae nobis adnuntiata sunt uaticinio prophetarum. tecit mirabilia: magum putassemus, ut et uos nunc putatis et Iudaei tunc putauerunt, si non illa ipsa facturum prophetae omnes uno spiritu praedixissent. itaque deum credimus non magis ex factis operibusque mirandis quam ex illa ipsa cruce, quam uos sicut canes lambitis, quoniam simul et illa praedicta est. non îgitur suo testimonio — cui enim de se dicenti potest credi? —, sed prophetarum testimonio, qui omnia quae fecit ac passus est multo ante cecinerunt, fidem diuinitatis accepit, quod neque Apollonio neque Apuleio neque cuiquam magorum potuit aut potest aliquando contingere. cum igitur talia ignorantiae suae deliramenta fudisset, cum ueritatem penitus excindere conisus esset, ausus est libros suos nefarios ac dei hostes φιλαληθεῖς; adnotare. o caecum pectus, o mentem Cimmeriis ut aiunt tenebris atrorem! discipulus hic fortasse Anaxagorae fuerit, cui niues atramentum fuerunt. atquin eadem caecitas est et uero falsitatis et mendacio ueritatis nomen inponere. uidelicet homo subdolus uoluit lupum sub ouis pelle celare, ut fallaci titulo posset in retire lectorem. uerum esto, inscitia hoc, non malitia feceris: quam tandem nobis adtulisti ueritatem, nisi quod adsertor deorum eos ipsos ad ultimum prodidisti? prosecutus enim summi dei laudes, quem regem, quem maximum, quem opificem rerum, quem fontem bonorum, quem parentem omnium, quem factorem altoremque uiuentium confessus es, ademisti Ioui tuo regnum eumque summa potestate depulsum in ministrorum numerum redegisti. epilogus itaque te tuus arguit stultitiae uanitatis erroris. adfirmas enim deos esse et illos tamen subicis et mancipas ei deo cuius religionem conaris euertere.
thought_title: Lactantius' Critique of Pagan Views on Christ
pass_a_gloss: Therefore, the will and cunning to fabricate were absent from these men, because they were unskilled. Or who can, being unlearned, fabricate things that are fitting and coherent with each other, when the most learned philosophers, Plato and Aristotle and Epicurus and Zeno, have themselves said things that are contradictory and opposed to each other? For this is the nature of falsehoods, that they cannot cohere. But the tradition of those men, because it is true, is consistent everywhere and entirely agrees with itself and therefore persuades, because it is supported by a consistent reason. Not, therefore, for the sake of gain or advantage did they invent this religion, since they themselves followed, both in precepts and in fact, a life that lacks pleasures and despises all things that are considered good, and who not only suffered death for the faith but also knew and predicted that they would die and that all who followed their teaching would suffer harsh and wicked things. But he affirmed that Christ, having been driven out by the Jews, had collected a band of nine hundred men and committed robberies. Who would dare to resist such great authority? Let us believe this plainly, for perhaps some Apollo or other announced this to them in their dreams. So many robbers have always perished and perish daily, and you yourself have condemned many of them: which of them, after their cross, is not called a god, but a man? But you perhaps believed this because you have consecrated a murderer, Mars, as a god: which you would not have done if the Areopagites had crucified him. When he was destroying the wonderful deeds of Christ, and yet not denying them, he wanted to show that Apollonius had done equal or even greater things. It is surprising that he passed over Apuleius, whose many and wonderful deeds are usually remembered. Why, therefore, does no one worship Apollonius as a god, except perhaps you alone, who are worthy of that god, with whom the true God will punish you in eternity? If Christ is a magician because he did wonderful things, then Apollonius is certainly more skilled, who, as you describe, when Domitian wanted to punish him, suddenly did not appear in court. How different from Christ, who was both seized and crucified. But perhaps he wanted to accuse Christ of arrogance from this very fact, that he constituted himself as God, so that Apollonius might seem more modest, who, although he did greater things, as he thinks, yet did not arrogate this to himself. I now omit comparing their works, because I spoke about the fraud and trickery of the magical art in the second and previous book. I deny that there is anyone who does not desire above all to attain after death what even the greatest kings desire. Why do men prepare for themselves magnificent tombs, why statues, why images? Why do they strive to earn the opinions of men by famous deeds or even by death on behalf of their citizens? Why, finally, did you want to establish this detestable monument of your intellect, built as it were on mud, unless you hope for immortality from the memory of your name? It is therefore foolish to think that Apollonius did not want what he would certainly desire if he could, because no one rejects immortality, especially since you say that he was even worshiped as a god by some and that a statue of his, under the name of Hercules Alexicacus, is still honored by the Ephesians. Therefore, he could not be believed to be a god after death, because it was established that he was a man and a magician, and so he affected divinity with the title of a foreign name, because he could not and did not dare with his own. But our Christ could be believed to be God, because he was not a magician, and he was believed, because he truly was. I do not say this because Apollonius is not considered a god, but because he did not want to be, in order that it may appear that we are wiser, who have not immediately added faith in divinity to wonderful deeds, as you have, who have believed a god because of small portents. It is not surprising if you, who are far removed from God's wisdom, do not understand at all what you have read, since the Jews, who from the beginning had read the prophets to whom the sacrament of God had been entrusted, yet did not know what they were reading. Learn, therefore, if you have any heart, that we do not believe Christ to be God because he did wonderful things, but because we saw that all things that were announced to us by the prophecy of the prophets were fulfilled in him. He passed over the wonderful deeds: we would have thought him a magician, as you now think and the Jews then thought, if all the prophets had not predicted beforehand, with one spirit, that he would do those very things. And so we believe him to be God, not so much because of his wonderful works, as because of that very cross, which you, like dogs, lick, since it too was predicted. Therefore, he did not receive the faith of divinity from his own testimony - for who can be believed when speaking about himself? - but from the testimony of the prophets, who sang beforehand, with one spirit, all that he did and suffered, which cannot happen to Apollonius or Apuleius or any of the magicians. When, therefore, he had poured out such delirious ravings of his ignorance, when he had tried to eradicate the truth entirely, he dared to entitle his books 'Truth-loving', a note of hostility to God. O blind heart, o mind filled with Cimmerian darkness, as they say! This man was perhaps a disciple of Anaxagoras, for whom snow was ink. But it is the same blindness to give the name of truth to falsehood and to impose the name of mendacity on truth. Clearly, a cunning man wanted to hide a wolf under a sheep's skin, so that with a deceitful title he could lead the reader astray. But let it be that you did this out of ignorance, not malice: what truth, then, have you brought to us, except that you, the defender of the gods, have ultimately betrayed them? For, having pursued the praises of the highest God, whom you confessed to be king, greatest, maker of things, fountain of goods, parent of all, creator and ruler of the living, you took away the kingdom from your Jupiter and reduced him to the number of servants, having deprived him of supreme power. Your epilogue, therefore, accuses you of the error of foolish vanity. For you affirm that there are gods, and yet you subject them to and make them servants of that God whose religion you try to overthrow.

pass_b_english: These men had no will to fabricate, nor any cunning to do so, because they were unskilled. Indeed, who could? An unlearned man cannot invent a coherent, self-consistent story when the most learned philosophers — Plato, Aristotle, Epicurus, and Zeno — contradicted one another and themselves. That is the nature of falsehoods: they cannot hold together. By contrast, the tradition these men handed down is true, so it is consistent at every point, entirely self-agreeing, and therefore persuasive, because it rests on a steady rational foundation. They did not invent this religion for profit or advantage. Their lives, both in precept and in practice, renounced pleasure and despised everything the world counts as good. They not only accepted death for their faith; they knew in advance they would die, they foretold it, and they warned that all who followed their teaching would suffer harsh and unspeakable things.

Yet the opponent affirms that Christ, driven out by the Jews, gathered a band of nine hundred men and turned bandit. Who dares challenge such authority? We are to believe it outright — perhaps some Apollo revealed it to him in a dream. Countless bandits have perished in the past and perish daily; you yourself have condemned many. Which of them, after his cross, was ever called not merely a man but a god? Perhaps you believed the story because you yourselves consecrated a murderer, Mars, as a god — something you would never have done had the Areopagites crucified him. While denying Christ’s wonders, the opponent tries to show that Apollonius performed equal or even greater feats. It is striking that he passes over Apuleius, whose many marvels are commonly recorded. Why, then, does no one worship Apollonius as a god — unless you alone, worthy of such a deity, with whom the true God will punish you for eternity? If Christ counts as a magician because he worked wonders, Apollonius is certainly the more skilled: when Domitian tried to punish him, he simply failed to appear in court. How different from Christ, who was seized and nailed to the cross. Perhaps the opponent means to charge Christ with arrogance for claiming to be God, so that Apollonius may seem more modest — though he allegedly did greater things, he did not arrogate divinity to himself.

I pass over a detailed comparison of their works now, having exposed the fraud and trickery of the magical art in the previous two books. I deny that anyone exists who does not desire above all to obtain after death what even the greatest kings crave. Why do men build magnificent tombs, erect statues, commission portraits? Why do they strive, through famous deeds or even death for their fellow citizens, to win the good opinion of posterity? Why, finally, did you choose to raise this detestable monument of your intellect, founded as it were on mud, unless you hope for immortality through the memory of your name? It is therefore foolish to suppose Apollonius did not want what he would certainly have desired if he could — for no one rejects immortality, especially when you admit that some worshiped him as a god and that his statue, under the name Hercules Alexicacus, is still honored by the Ephesians. He could not be believed a god after death, because it was established he was a man and a magician; thus he laid claim to divinity under a foreign title, since he could not and dared not do so in his own name. But our Christ could be believed God because he was no magician, and he was believed because he truly was God. I do not say this to prove Apollonius is not a god because he refused the title, but to show that we are wiser: we do not instantly ascribe divinity to marvels, as you do, who accepted a god on the strength of petty portents.

It is no wonder that you, so far removed from God’s wisdom, understand nothing of what you have read. The Jews, who from the beginning had read the prophets to whom God’s mystery was entrusted, still did not know what they were reading. Learn, then, if you have any heart: we do not believe Christ is God because he worked wonders, but because we saw that everything the prophets foretold was fulfilled in him. He passed over the wonders: we would have taken him for a magician, as you do now and the Jews did then, had not all the prophets, with one spirit, predicted beforehand that he would do those very things. And so we believe him God not so much because of his wondrous works as because of that very cross, which you lick like dogs — since the cross, too, was foretold. He did not receive the faith of divinity from his own testimony — for who can be believed when speaking of himself? — but from the testimony of the prophets, who sang long before, with one spirit, all that he did and suffered. That can never happen for Apollonius, Apuleius, or any magician.

After pouring out such delirious ravings of ignorance, after trying to uproot the truth entirely, he dared to title his books ‘Truth-loving’ — a label hostile to God. O blind heart, O mind blacker than Cimmerian darkness! He may have been a disciple of Anaxagoras, for whom snow served as ink. But it is the same blindness to call falsehood truth and to brand truth as mendacity. Clearly a crafty man sought to hide a wolf under a sheep’s skin, that with a deceitful title he might lead the reader astray. Yet grant it was ignorance, not malice: what truth have you brought us, except that you, the defender of the gods, have in the end betrayed them? You heaped praise on the highest God — confessing him King, Greatest, Maker of all, Fountain of good, Parent of all, Creator and Sustainer of the living — then you stripped your own Jupiter of his kingdom and reduced him to the rank of a servant, deprived of supreme power. Your own epilogue therefore convicts you of the error of foolish vanity. You affirm that gods exist, yet you subject them and enslave them to the very God whose religion you try to overthrow.
